note: Original flora, batch 2 of 3: herbs, spices, aromatics and dye plants. Each entry is written for Asetheria; the real plant it is grounded in is named in the DM notes under 'Basis'. No third-party text is reproduced.

entries.name: Hymettan Thyme
entries.summary: Low aromatic scrub of the dry hills, the flower that gives the bees of the highlands their honey.
entries.body:
A low, grey-green, wiry herb that carpets the dry hills in a purple haze in early summer. The bees that feed on it make a dark, fragrant honey that the coast prizes above all others, and the plant itself flavours meat, flavours oil, and goes into a smoky incense for the hearth gods.

## Where it is found

Its best fields cover the hills above [[Kirimitsana]], where the beekeepers of the mountain town set their hives in a long row.

## In play

A bundle of thyme in the bed-linen is said to bring good dreams and drive off fleas. The honey it makes is a gift fit for a magistrate. Bees that have fed on it are slow and docile in the evening, an advantage for any raider hoping to rob a hive.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real Greek thyme (Thymbra capitata and related thymes), whose nectar produces the famous honey of Mount Hymettus near Athens; thyme was used as flavouring, incense and a fumigant.

fields.effects:
• Bees on thyme make a dark, fragrant honey.
• A sprig in bedding drives off fleas.
• Burned as a smoky household incense.
fields.lore: A gift of thyme honey is how a poor man thanks a rich one without lowering himself.

entries.name: Witch's Rue
entries.summary: A bitter, blue-grey herb used as an antidote, a charm against the evil eye, and an abortifacient with a hard reputation.
entries.body:
A bushy plant with blue-green lobed leaves and a harsh, bitter smell, grown in every herb garden for its reputation. Rue is a hundred things at once: a flavouring, a guard against the evil eye, an antidote to poisons, a charm against witches, a cure for sore eyes. Rubbed on skin it can blister, and taken wrongly it can harm.

## Where it is found

It grows in the walled herb-gardens of [[Aeterna City]] and wild on the dry slopes of the [[Klynin Mountain Range]].

## In play

A sprig is the standard charm against the evil eye and sells for a copper. In a healer's hands it is a medicine (Medicine, DC 12) and in careless ones, a poison. Its sap can raise a rash on bare skin, which is the same stuff that gave it its mystique.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real rue (Ruta graveolens), prized by Greeks and Romans as an antidote and charm and a flavouring; contact with the sap can cause photodermatitis and large doses are toxic.

fields.effects:
• Carried as a charm against the evil eye.
• In a healer's hands, an antidote to some poisons.
• Sap blisters bare skin; large doses poison.
fields.lore: The Imperial saying: rue is a friend to the wise and an enemy to the clever.

entries.name: Temple Hyssop
entries.summary: A small bitter herb used as a sprinkler for ritual cleansing and as a medicine for the cough.
entries.body:
A small bushy herb with spikes of blue flowers and a camphor scent. Bundled and dipped in water, it is the priest's sprinkler: a few flicks over a doorway or a sickroom purifies the place in the eyes of the gods. Steeped in honey it is the grandmother's cure for the cough.

## Where it is found

It grows in the dry stony ground around [[Mithratal City]] and the sanctuary terraces of [[Delphara City]].

## In play

A priest with a bundle of hyssop can ritually cleanse a person or a place, which many communities require after a death or a crime. The tea eases a cough and soothes the chest. A character who needs a cover story for a night-time visit to a shrine does well to carry some.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real hyssop (Hyssopus officinalis, or a similar aromatic Near Eastern herb), used in ritual purification in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East and as a cough remedy.

fields.effects:
• A bundle dipped in water sprinkles ritual cleansing.
• Tea with honey eases a cough.
• Camphor-scented and bitter.
fields.lore: Priests say a house sprinkled with hyssop cannot hide a guilty heart.

entries.name: Sea-Wormwood
entries.summary: Silver-grey bitter herb steeped to expel worms, to flavour vermouth, and to curse a drunkard.
entries.body:
A silvery, aromatic perennial whose leaves taste so bitter they pucker the whole face. It is the apothecary's staple against worms and fever, the brewer's flavouring for a harsh herbal wine, and the sort of thing a mother threatens a naughty child with. The word is a byword for bitterness in every empire.

## Where it is found

It grows on the salt-marsh margins of the [[Maeotis Helos]] and the dry banks of the [[Latium Plains]].

## In play

A cup of wormwood tea clears intestinal parasites in three days. A wine infused with it is a drink for the sturdy. Taken in excess it brings tremors and a wild mind, and a heavy drinker of it is a recognisable figure in the taverns.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), a bitter herb used in antiquity as a vermifuge and tonic and to flavour wine (Pliny mentions wormwood wine); thujone in large amounts is toxic.

fields.effects:
• Tea clears intestinal worms in three days.
• Infused wine is a bitter tonic.
• Excess causes tremors and a wild mind.
fields.lore: A child told 'wormwood' knows to stop whatever it is doing.

entries.name: Saviour's Sage
entries.summary: Grey-green herb whose name means to heal, steeped for sore throats and strewn on the floors of the sick.
entries.body:
A soft grey-green leaf with a heavy resinous smell, grown in every garden for its reputation. A tea of it eases a sore throat, a pinch in broth is thought to sharpen the wits, and the elderly keep a pot on the windowsill against the ills of winter. Its Hellenorian name literally means that which saves.

## Where it is found

It grows in the kitchen gardens of [[Helionyx City]] and wild in the hills of the [[Olympus Mountain Range]].

## In play

A cup of sage tea restores a few hit points to a sore-throated character and lets them speak at full volume. A good healer is easily recognised by the pot at the door. It is common enough that it would be remarkable to find an apothecary without it.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real sage (Salvia officinalis), whose Latin name (salvare, to save) reflects its medicinal reputation; used by Greeks and Romans for throat and digestion and as a general tonic.

fields.effects:
• Tea eases a sore throat.
• Added to broth as a tonic for the old.
• A pot at the door marks a healer.
fields.lore: A wise woman keeps sage and a short temper.

entries.name: Sweet Marjoram
entries.summary: Fragrant garden herb that grows over graves, perfumes the lovers' bed and scents the oils of the baths.
entries.body:
A soft, sweet-smelling herb with small rounded leaves, grown in pots and borders for its perfume. In myth the goddess of love breathed on it and gave it its scent; in practice every bath-house in the Imperium keeps a jar of its oil. A wreath of it is hung over the doors of newlyweds, and the same plant, in another corner of the world, is planted over graves.

## Where it is found

It grows in the herb-beds of [[Romulo City]] and the bath-house gardens of [[Aeterna City]].

## In play

Marjoram oil rubbed into the temples eases a headache (advantage on one Constitution save against exhaustion from the pain). It is a gentle, harmless herb, and a character who needs an innocent cover for hours of slow cooking has found it.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real marjoram (Origanum majorana), a fragrant herb associated with Aphrodite/Venus in Greek and Roman tradition and used in perfumes, cooking and for healing.

fields.effects:
• Oil eases a tension headache.
• Wreaths are hung over newlyweds' doors.
• A staple scent in bath-houses.
fields.lore: Gardeners say it grows sweeter the more it is cut and the less it is praised.

entries.name: Bug-Herb
entries.summary: A leafy herb that smells of bedbugs when young and of lemon when ripe, grown for its seed and its smell.
entries.body:
A feathery green herb whose fresh leaves are unmistakably pungent: the Hellenorians named it for the smell of a bedbug. The seed that follows is warm and citrus-sweet and is the base of half the spice mixes on the coast. A little goes into bread, wine and the poultices of the old.

## Where it is found

It grows in the market gardens of [[Argotiko]] and the dry fields beyond [[Qa'zshahrv'in]].

## In play

A pinch of ground seed in a stew is the Hellenorian touch. Those who dislike the fresh leaf dislike it a great deal; a character with a strong opinion on the matter is nobody to cross at dinner.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real coriander (Coriandrum sativum), whose Greek name koris refers to a bedbug; both leaves and seed were used in ancient cooking and medicine, and it is recorded in the Linear B tablets.

fields.effects:
• Ground seed flavours bread, wine and stew.
• Fresh leaves smell strongly to some.
• A mild digestive.
fields.lore: Love it or leave the table: there is no middle ground.

entries.name: Caravan Cumin
entries.summary: A warm brown seed ground into stew, bread and the cheap spice that every poor kitchen has.
entries.body:
A small, slender annual that gives a brown, ridged, warm-smelling seed, and the cheapest spice a poor kitchen can buy. The caravans carry it in sacks as ballast, and the cooks of the plateau throw a pinch into every pot. A miser is called a cumin-splitter, from the man who divides a seed to save a seed.

## Where it is found

It is grown on the dry fields around [[Atarabad City]] and the caravan towns beyond.

## In play

A small pouch of cumin makes a pot of lentils edible. In powder, it can be blown in a face to cause a fit of sneezing (a Constitution saving throw, DC 11, or lose the next action). A character who eats it daily has no trouble with the road stew.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real cumin (Cuminum cyminum), a staple spice across the Mediterranean and Near East; Greek and Roman writers called a very stingy man a 'cumin-splitter'.

fields.effects:
• Ground seed flavours stews and bread.
• Powder blown in the face causes a sneezing fit.
• Cheap and ubiquitous.
fields.lore: A cumin-splitter is the name for a man who would count the beans in a bowl.

entries.name: Torch-Fennel
entries.summary: A giant fennel whose dry stalk burns slowly and carries a coal from camp to camp: the first tinder-box.
entries.body:
A towering fennel that can reach ten feet, with a thick hollow stalk full of dry pith. Lit at one end, the pith smoulders for hours and can carry a glowing coal in a pocket from one camp to the next. The myth says a god stole fire from heaven in such a stalk.

## Where it is found

It grows on the dry slopes of the [[Oros Mountain Range]] and the rocky banks above [[Corinth City]].

## In play

A cut and dried stalk carries a coal for six hours in a leather case. The plant is poisonous to livestock in some varieties, which a farmer learns once. A traveller who needs to move fire and has no tinderbox can improvise one in an hour (Survival, DC 11).
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real giant fennel (Ferula communis, the narthex), whose dry pith smoulders slowly and was used to carry fire; in Greek myth Prometheus stole fire from the gods in a fennel stalk.

fields.effects:
• A dried stalk carries a coal for hours.
• Some varieties poison livestock.
• Ten feet tall; visible from afar.
fields.lore: Children are told that the first fire came down in a stalk of it, and have never fully recovered.

entries.name: Cooling Mint
entries.summary: Strong-scented herb that sours milk, scents tables and is rubbed on benches before guests arrive.
entries.body:
A fast-spreading herb with square stems and a cool, sharp smell. In the old tales a nymph was trampled and turned into it, and a hearty smell is her last complaint. Hosts rub it on the table before a feast, cooks use it to cut a heavy sauce, and herbalists use it to ease a stomach.

## Where it is found

It runs wild along the damp places of the [[River Tiberius]] and the garden terraces of [[Persevalis City]].

## In play

Chewed fresh, it clears the breath and the nose. A warm tea settles a queasy stomach (advantage on one Constitution save against being sick). It spreads to cover any bed it is planted in, and a gardener who has planted it once regrets it.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real mint (Mentha spicata and relatives), used by Greeks and Romans for scenting tables and in sauces and medicine; in myth the nymph Minthe was transformed into the plant.

fields.effects:
• Tea settles a queasy stomach.
• Rubbed on tables to scent a feast.
• Spreads over any bed it is planted in.
fields.lore: A host who forgets the mint is a host who forgets the guest.

entries.name: Trade Cassia
entries.summary: Rolled bark of an eastern tree, a warm, sweet spice carried half a world at a price the poor cannot imagine.
entries.body:
The inner bark of a far eastern tree, dried until it curls into a stick the colour of a polished saddle. Sweet, warm and faintly peppery, it perfumes the court, flavours the finest wine, and goes into the anointing oil of kings. It arrives on the coast after a journey so long and so costly that a few sticks are a sum.

## Where it is found

It reaches the continent only through the bazaar of [[Persemenid City]] and is sold on to the nobility of [[Hellarchon City]].

## In play

A pouch of cassia is a gift fit for a magistrate. Travellers tell tall stories about its origin: the spice-sellers cheerfully invent them to keep the price high, and a character who can see through the lie (Insight, DC 13) knows it grows on a tree like any other.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real cassia (Cinnamomum cassia), a cinnamon-like bark from East Asia traded through the Near East; ancient writers told elaborate tall tales about its origin (such as harvesting from cinnamon-birds' nests) to protect the trade.

fields.effects:
• A few sticks scent a feast and flavour a rich wine.
• Used in anointing oil.
• Its true origin is a closely guarded trade secret.
fields.lore: The spice-sellers say it grows in the nests of great birds, and charge accordingly.

entries.name: Black Pepper
entries.summary: Dried berries from a distant climbing vine, worth their weight in silver and counted out peppercorn by peppercorn.
entries.body:
A glossy climbing vine bears clusters of green berries that are dried until they wrinkle black and hard. Pungent and sharp, a few grains transform a dull dish, and the merchants who carry it across the sea sell it to the rich by the pound and to the poor by the grain. A city can be ransomed in peppercorns, and was.

## Where it is found

It arrives at the docks of [[Hellarchon City]] and [[Fucostia]] by long-haul ship, and is stored in guarded warehouses.

## In play

A pound of pepper is worth many pounds of silver and is a standard portable treasure. A shipment diverted is a serious loss and a good heist. A plain cook who has used a whole peppercorn knows how much money is in her mortar.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real black pepper (Piper nigrum), a spice from India that was among the most valuable trade goods of the Roman world; Alaric is recorded demanding 3,000 pounds of pepper in the ransom of Rome.

fields.effects:
• Worth its weight in silver.
• A few grains transform a dull dish.
• A cargo of it is a portable fortune.
fields.lore: A ransom in peppercorns is the polite form of extortion.

entries.name: Root of Warmth
entries.summary: A knobbled, pungent root brought from the far south, steeped against cold and a queasy sea.
entries.body:
A knobbly, tan root that is peeled and sliced to reveal a pale yellow flesh with a hot, sharp, sweet taste. Sailors chew it against seasickness and soldiers steep it against cold, and the Imperium's great banquets serve it candied. A small piece cuts the chill of a wet night.

## Where it is found

It comes in dried stems on the long sea road and is stocked in the spice-sellers of [[Fucostia]] and [[Aeterna City]].

## In play

A piece chewed on a rolling deck ends seasickness. A hot infusion gives advantage on a saving throw against the first stage of exposure to cold. It travels well and keeps for a year, so a trader's pack of dry root is a safe investment.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real ginger (Zingiber officinale), imported into the Roman world and used as a spice and for digestion and chills; Dioscorides and Pliny mention it.

fields.effects:
• Chewed root ends seasickness.
• A hot infusion helps against the first stage of cold.
• Keeps for a year when dried.
fields.lore: A sailor without ginger is a sailor who will soon be seasick, and fervent.

entries.name: Red-Root Madder
entries.summary: A straggling plant whose roots, boiled and ground, give the red of soldiers' cloaks and the stains of drinkers' teeth.
entries.body:
A scrambling, rough-stemmed plant that clambers over hedges and fences. Its long orange roots are dug, dried, ground and boiled to give the best red dye of the old world: the red of a legion's cloak and of the cheap woollens of a thousand villages. Cattle that eat it have red bones and red milk, and a farmer finds out.

## Where it is found

It is grown in long beds near [[Tabrishi'ir]] and on the clay fields around [[Mavelon City]].

## In play

A cloth dyed with madder is the standard soldier's red and holds its colour for years. A dyer's hands are stained to the wrist, and a character with red hands who denies working in the dye-house is lying.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real madder (Rubia tinctorum), the root dye behind the red of Roman military cloaks and Persian carpets; its pigment tints the bones and milk of animals that eat it.

fields.effects:
• Root yields a durable red dye.
• Dyer's hands stay stained for weeks.
• Animals that eat it have red bones and milk.
fields.lore: Weavers of the plateau say a carpet is only as good as its red.

entries.name: Warrior's Woad
entries.summary: A yellow-flowered herb fermented into blue dye, painted on skin by the fierce and on wool by the patient.
entries.body:
A leafy herb with clusters of tiny yellow flowers. Its leaves, crushed and left to rot in a vat, give up a blue dye that is deeper and more lasting than any other. The fermentation is foul-smelling and the dyers' quarter is always the poorest and most stinking, but the blue it makes is worth the stench. Painted raw on skin it dries to a fierce bruise-colour.

## Where it is found

It grows in the cold fields of the north and is sold from the [[Foloicauria Forest]] borderlands to the dyers of [[Aeterna City]].

## In play

A warrior with woad-painted arms is a fierce neighbour. The dye is slow, smelly work. Dyers make their living by patience and a bad sense of smell, and each guild keeps its vats a trade secret.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real woad (Isatis tinctoria), the European source of blue dye before indigo; Caesar recorded that the Britons stained themselves with vitrum (woad), and fermentation of the leaves is notoriously foul-smelling.

fields.effects:
• Fermented leaves make a lasting blue dye.
• Painted raw, it stains skin dark blue.
• The dyers' vats stink for a mile.
fields.lore: The north's gift to the south is a blue that outlasts the wearer.

entries.name: Yellow Weld
entries.summary: A slender roadside weed that gives the sun-bright yellow of wedding veils and festival robes.
entries.body:
A tall, slim, yellow-green weed of waste ground and roadsides. Cut in flower and boiled, it gives a fast, brilliant yellow that is the colour of the flame-veil worn by the bride of the Imperium and of the festival robes of its priestesses. A dyer who wants green dips the cloth in woad first.

## Where it is found

It springs up in every neglected field along the roads of the [[Latium Plains]] and the waste ground outside [[Romulo City]].

## In play

A length of weld-dyed silk is a bride's treasure. A dyer who needs a rich green knows the trick of mixing weld and woad. Foragers can cut a good armful in an hour and sell it for a few coppers.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real weld (Reseda luteola), the main yellow dye of the ancient and medieval Old World; the flammeum, the Roman bride's veil, was a bright saffron-yellow-orange.

fields.effects:
• Yields a fast, bright yellow dye.
• With woad it gives a rich green.
• Easily foraged along any road.
fields.lore: The bride's yellow comes from the weed her mother pulled from the garden wall.

entries.name: Red-Hand Leaf
entries.summary: A shrub whose ground leaves paint hands, nails and hair a rich rust-red, and bless a bride.
entries.body:
A thin, many-branched shrub with small pale leaves that are dried and ground to a fine green powder. Mixed with water it makes a paste that stains skin, nails, hair and the manes of horses a warm rust-red that lasts for weeks. Brides have their palms painted before the wedding, and the old paint their white hair against age.

## Where it is found

It grows in the hot gardens of [[Atarabad City]] and the oases of the [[Dasht-a Khaliq]].

## In play

A bride's painted hands are a mark of the day and of a family's means. The stain also marks a character who has recently been to a wedding, a very good alibi or a very bad one. The cooling paste eases a fever on the soles of the feet.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real henna (Lawsonia inermis), whose ground leaves make a reddish-orange dye used for skin and hair across the Near East since antiquity, including at weddings.

fields.effects:
• Paste stains skin, nails and hair rust-red for weeks.
• A bride's palms are painted before the wedding.
• A cooling paste eases a fever.
fields.lore: A bride's hands are the only fresh ink in a family's history.

entries.name: Poor Man's Saffron
entries.summary: A thistly orange flower whose petals dye silk red and stand in for the costlier crocus.
entries.body:
A tall, spiny thistle with brilliant orange flower heads. The petals are picked, dried and used to dye cloth a warm orange-red and to colour food the gold that only saffron should give. Cooks who cannot afford the true spice use it; fraudulent merchants who sell it as the true spice are punished when caught.

## Where it is found

It is grown in dry fields near [[Tabrishi'ir]] and sold in the bazaar of [[Persevalis City]].

## In play

A customer who suspects fraud can tell the real saffron from the false by the tint it gives to water (Investigation, DC 13). Its seeds yield a useful lamp oil. A merchant caught passing off the poor man's saffron as the real one is fined and shamed.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real safflower (Carthamus tinctorius), used since antiquity for dye and as a cheap substitute for saffron; its seeds yield an edible and lamp oil.

fields.effects:
• Petals dye cloth orange-red.
• A cheap, fraudulent stand-in for saffron.
• Seeds yield lamp oil.
fields.lore: A cook who cannot afford crocus plants a thistle and hopes.

entries.name: Mountain Spikenard
entries.summary: A hairy mountain root ground into an ointment so costly that one jar can anoint a king or a corpse and ruin a household.
entries.body:
A small, hairy, spiky root from a far northern slope, ground and steeped into an oil with a heavy, sweet, earthy fragrance. A single jar is enough to anoint a king; it is also the oil a grieving woman pours over a beloved's feet, and a rich widow once poured out a year's wages in one gesture. It is sold in tiny sealed alabaster flasks.

## Where it is found

The root is dug on the high slopes beyond the [[Cloudspine Ridge]] and brought down by a few families who guard the secret.

## In play

A flask is a fortune in a small package. An oath sworn over spikenard oil is not to be broken. A character in the middle of a grand gesture can use it; a pickpocket who steals the flask learns how little a stolen fortune is worth if no one will buy it.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real spikenard (Nardostachys jatamansi), a Himalayan root made into a costly perfume oil in antiquity; the Gospel accounts describe a woman anointing Jesus with nard worth a year's wages.

fields.effects:
• A flask is a fortune.
• Used to anoint the king and the dead.
• An oath over it is binding.
fields.lore: A widow pours it on the feet of her beloved, and the neighbours count the cost for years.

entries.name: Balm of the Hill Country
entries.summary: A rare scented shrub whose cut bark yields a drop of healing balm, guarded in walled gardens and sold by the thimble.
entries.body:
A small, scrubby tree with aromatic leaves, grown nowhere but a few walled gardens on a single hillside. Its bark is cut with a stone knife and the sap collected drop by drop in horn spoons. The balm heals wounds, scents the court, and is such a treasure that conquerors have demanded the gardens as tribute.

## Where it is found

Its walled gardens lie in the foothills of the [[Klynin Mountain Range]], watched by soldiers and by a priesthood.

## In play

A few drops of the balm applied to a wound restores 1d8 hit points once per long rest, to a patient who rests an hour. A conqueror who takes the gardens and does not take the gardeners ends up with dead trees. The guards allow nobody with a knife past the gate.
entries.dmNotes: Basis: real balm of Gilead / opobalsamum (Commiphora gileadensis), a rare aromatic shrub whose resin was among the most costly medicinal and perfume products of antiquity, grown in a few guarded plantations (as at Jericho and Ein Gedi).

fields.effects:
• A few drops dress a wound (1d8 hit points once per long rest).
• Worth far more than gold by weight.
• Only the gardeners know how to tap it without killing the shrub.
fields.lore: Conquerors demand it as tribute, and learn why the gardeners are never named in the treaty.
